levels.title: Logic in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what logic and critical thinking do: check whether the reasons for a claim really support it.

levels.title: What Counts as an Argument
levels.objective: After this level you can tell an argument, a set of reasons offered for a claim, from a quarrel, a story or a bare opinion.

levels.title: Claims: True or False
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a claim is and why only claims, not questions or commands, can be true or false.

levels.title: Fact, Opinion or Value?
levels.objective: After this level you can sort a statement into a checkable fact, a personal taste or a value judgment.

levels.title: Premises and Conclusions
levels.objective: After this level you can name the premises and the conclusion of a simple argument.

levels.title: Finding the Conclusion
levels.objective: After this level you can use signal words like "therefore", "so" and "because" to find an argument's conclusion.

levels.title: The Unstated Premise
levels.objective: After this level you can spot the hidden assumption an argument needs but never says out loud.

levels.title: Explaining Isn't Arguing
levels.objective: After this level you can tell an explanation of why something happened from an argument that something is true.

levels.title: Arguments in Chains
levels.objective: After this level you can trace how one argument's conclusion becomes the premise of the next.

levels.title: Checkpoint: What an Argument Is
levels.objective: After this level you can take an everyday argument apart into its claims, premises, hidden assumptions and conclusion.

levels.title: Deduction
levels.objective: After this level you can explain deduction: reasoning in which true premises guarantee a true conclusion.

levels.title: Valid Doesn't Mean True
levels.objective: After this level you can explain validity and why a valid argument can still reach a false conclusion.

levels.title: Soundness
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why an argument needs both a valid form and true premises to be sound.

levels.title: The Syllogism
levels.objective: After this level you can test an "all" and "some" argument of the kind Aristotle first studied, using overlapping circles.

levels.title: If This, Then That
levels.objective: After this level you can use the two valid if-then forms: affirming the "if" part and denying the "then" part.

levels.title: The Backwards If
levels.objective: After this level you can spot the two tempting invalid if-then forms: affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent.

levels.title: Induction
levels.objective: After this level you can explain induction: reasoning from examples to a conclusion that is probable, not certain.

levels.title: The Black Swan Problem
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why no number of confirming cases proves a generalization, while one counterexample can sink it.

levels.title: Reasoning Like a Detective
levels.objective: After this level you can explain inference to the best explanation: choosing the account that best fits all the clues.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Deduction and Induction
levels.objective: After this level you can compare deduction, induction and best-explanation reasoning and say how much certainty each gives.

levels.title: What a Fallacy Is
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what a fallacy is and why a bad argument can still feel convincing.

levels.title: Attacking the Person
levels.objective: After this level you can spot an ad hominem, which attacks the arguer instead of the argument.

levels.title: The Straw Man
levels.objective: After this level you can spot a straw man, which knocks down a weaker version of someone's view instead of the real one.

levels.title: The False Choice
levels.objective: After this level you can spot a false dilemma that hides the options beyond the two on offer.

levels.title: The Slippery Slope
levels.objective: After this level you can judge a slippery slope argument by checking how likely each step really is.

levels.title: Going in Circles
levels.objective: After this level you can spot circular reasoning, where the conclusion is quietly assumed in the premises.

levels.title: The Red Herring
levels.objective: After this level you can spot a red herring that changes the subject while seeming to answer it.

levels.title: "What About You?"
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why pointing out someone's hypocrisy doesn't answer their argument.

levels.title: Everyone Believes It
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a claim's popularity is not, by itself, evidence that it is true.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Classic Fallacies
levels.objective: After this level you can name the classic fallacies and explain how each one dodges, distorts or assumes the point.

levels.title: What Counts as Evidence
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what makes something evidence for a claim rather than just a reason to like it.

levels.title: Who Has to Prove It?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the burden of proof and why it falls on the person making the claim.

levels.title: Not Found Isn't Disproved
levels.objective: After this level you can explain when a lack of evidence counts against a claim and when it proves nothing.

levels.title: "It Worked for Me"
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why one vivid personal story is weak evidence about what usually happens.

levels.title: Jumping to Conclusions
levels.objective: After this level you can spot a hasty generalization drawn from too few or unusual cases.

levels.title: Cherry-Picking
levels.objective: After this level you can spot cherry-picking, where only the evidence that helps the case is shown.

levels.title: Only the Survivors
levels.objective: After this level you can explain survivorship bias, using the damaged planes that made it home from war.

levels.title: Extraordinary Claims
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a surprising claim needs stronger evidence than an ordinary one.

levels.title: When Evidence Converges
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why independent lines of evidence that agree are stronger than any one alone.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Weighing Evidence
levels.objective: After this level you can rank evidence from weak to strong and explain what makes the difference.

levels.title: What Makes a Cause
levels.objective: After this level you can explain a cause as something that makes a difference: without it, the effect would not have happened.

levels.title: Correlation Isn't Causation
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why two things rising and falling together doesn't show that one causes the other.

levels.title: After This, So Because of This?
levels.objective: After this level you can spot the post hoc fallacy, which treats "came first" as "caused it".

levels.title: The Hidden Third Factor
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a confounder, like hot weather, can drive two things at once and fake a link between them.

levels.title: Which Way Does It Run?
levels.objective: After this level you can spot reverse causation, where the supposed effect is really the cause.

levels.title: Just a Coincidence?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why, given enough chances, surprising coincidences are bound to happen.

levels.title: More Than One Cause
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why most events have several causes and why blaming only one misleads.

levels.title: Necessary or Sufficient?
levels.objective: After this level you can tell a necessary condition from a sufficient one.

levels.title: When the Measure Becomes the Goal
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Goodhart's law: why a number stops measuring well once people are rewarded for hitting it.

levels.title: Milestone: Reasons, Evidence and Causes
levels.objective: After this level you can connect arguments, evidence and causes into one method for checking a claim.

levels.title: Looking Only for Yes
levels.objective: After this level you can explain confirmation bias and counter it by looking for evidence that could prove you wrong.

levels.title: Believing What We Want
levels.objective: After this level you can explain motivated reasoning: starting from the answer you want and working backward to reasons.

levels.title: The Double Standard
levels.objective: After this level you can use the switch-sides test: would you accept this argument if it backed the opposite conclusion?

levels.title: Natural Isn't Always Better
levels.objective: After this level you can spot the appeal to nature: assuming something is good or safe just because it is natural.

levels.title: Perfect or Nothing
levels.objective: After this level you can spot the perfect-solution fallacy: rejecting an idea because it doesn't solve the whole problem.

levels.title: Sounding Sure Isn't Evidence
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a confident, fluent delivery is not a reason to believe a claim.

levels.title: Patterns in Noise
levels.objective: After this level you can spot the Texas sharpshooter fallacy: drawing the target around the bullet holes after the fact.

levels.title: The Bias Blind Spot
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why people spot bias in others far more easily than in themselves.

levels.title: "We've Always Done It This Way"
levels.objective: After this level you can spot the appeal to tradition and explain when a long track record is, and isn't, a good reason.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Traps in Our Reasoning
levels.objective: After this level you can name the reasoning traps that catch careful people and a habit that counters each one.

levels.title: What Makes Science Different
levels.objective: After this level you can explain science as a way of testing ideas against the world and correcting its own mistakes.

levels.title: Could It Be Proved Wrong?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Karl Popper's idea that a scientific claim must be falsifiable.

levels.title: Hypothesis, Prediction, Test
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the logic of a scientific test: a hypothesis predicts something, and a failed prediction counts against it.

levels.title: A Theory Isn't a Guess
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what scientists mean by a theory, and why "just a theory" misunderstands the word.

levels.title: Saving a Theory at Any Cost
levels.objective: After this level you can spot an ad hoc rescue: an excuse invented only to protect a claim from evidence against it.

levels.title: When You Can't Experiment
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how scientists showed that smoking causes lung cancer without experimenting on people.

levels.title: Peer Review
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what peer review checks before a study is published, and what it can miss.

levels.title: How Science Changes Its Mind
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how new evidence overturned accepted ideas, such as bacteria causing most stomach ulcers.

levels.title: Spotting Pseudoscience
levels.objective: After this level you can spot pseudoscience by its untestable claims and its habit of moving the goalposts.

levels.title: Checkpoint: How Science Tests Ideas
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how controls, blinding, randomizing and replication turn a hunch into knowledge.

levels.title: Three Ways to Persuade
levels.objective: After this level you can identify appeals to character, emotion and reason: Aristotle's ethos, pathos and logos.

levels.title: Appeals to Emotion
levels.objective: After this level you can tell when emotion is relevant to a decision and when it stands in for the reasons.

levels.title: Loaded Words
levels.objective: After this level you can spot how word choice, like "used" versus "pre-owned", tilts a claim before any argument is made.

levels.title: Same Fact, Different Frame
levels.objective: After this level you can explain framing: why "90 percent survive" and "10 percent die" feel different but say the same thing.

levels.title: Weasel Words
levels.objective: After this level you can spot vague words like "up to" and "helps" that make a claim sound bigger than it is.

levels.title: The Loaded Question
levels.objective: After this level you can spot a loaded question that smuggles in an assumption you never agreed to.

levels.title: One Word, Two Meanings
levels.objective: After this level you can spot equivocation, where an argument quietly switches the meaning of a key word halfway through.

levels.title: No True Scotsman
levels.objective: After this level you can spot the move that redefines a group to wave away a counterexample.

levels.title: Persuasion or Manipulation?
levels.objective: After this level you can tell persuasion that gives you good reasons from manipulation that works around them.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Persuasion and Rhetoric
levels.objective: After this level you can take apart a persuasive message and separate its reasons from its techniques.

levels.title: When to Trust an Expert
levels.objective: After this level you can tell real expertise from a false appeal to authority, such as an expert speaking outside their field.

levels.title: Who Benefits?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh a conflict of interest without dismissing a claim just because of who made it.

levels.title: Straight From the Source
levels.objective: After this level you can tell a primary source from a secondhand retelling and explain why details drift as a claim is passed on.

levels.title: Consensus and the Lone Dissenter
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a field's consensus usually outweighs one contrarian expert, and how consensus can still change.

levels.title: Occam's Razor
levels.objective: After this level you can use Occam's razor to prefer the explanation that needs the fewest extra assumptions.

levels.title: Weighing a Conspiracy Claim
levels.objective: After this level you can judge a conspiracy claim by whether it could be tested and how many people would have to keep the secret.

levels.title: From Study to Headline
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a cautious finding in one study can grow into a bold headline, and how to check it.

levels.title: Echo Chambers
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how hearing only agreeing sources makes a view feel more certain than the evidence allows.

levels.title: A Real Photo, the Wrong Story
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a real photo or video proves only what it shows, and check whether it is being used out of context.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Judging Sources and Claims
levels.objective: After this level you can decide how much to trust a claim by weighing who says it, what backs it and what else could explain it.

levels.title: Good Decision, Bad Outcome
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why a decision should be judged by what was known at the time, not only by how it turned out.

levels.title: The Sunk Cost Trap
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why money or time already spent should not decide what you do next.

levels.title: Thinking One Step Further
levels.objective: After this level you can use second-order thinking to spot the side effects and knock-on effects of a decision.

levels.title: Imagine It Failed
levels.objective: After this level you can run a pre-mortem: imagine a plan has already failed, then work out why, to find its weak points in advance.

levels.title: How Sure Are You?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain calibration: matching how confident you feel to how often you turn out to be right.

levels.title: Changing Your Mind
levels.objective: After this level you can update a belief in proportion to new evidence, rather than all at once or not at all.

levels.title: The Steel Man
levels.objective: After this level you can build the strongest version of a view you disagree with before you answer it.

levels.title: Myths About Logic
levels.objective: After this level you can debunk myths about logic, like "a fallacy proves the conclusion false" or "you can't prove a negative".

levels.title: Your Thinking Toolkit
levels.objective: After this level you can run a new claim through the tree's key checks: the argument, the evidence, the cause, your own biases and the source.

levels.title: Mastery Challenge: Logic & Critical Thinking
levels.objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Logic & Critical Thinking Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
